stem: When the agent calls `lookup_order` and sees the item was purchased 45 days ago, how does the agentic loop decide whether to call `process_refund` or `escalate_to_human` next?

options.label: A
options.body: The order details are appended to the conversation and the model reasons about which action to take.
options.rationale: Correct. The agentic loop appends `tool_result` messages to the conversation and lets the model choose the next step each turn — that's how 45 days → refund vs. escalate gets resolved.

options.label: B
options.body: The agent follows a pre-configured decision tree mapping order attributes to tool calls.
options.rationale: Agentic loops are model-driven, not decision-tree-driven. Hardcoded trees are the opposite of the pattern.

options.label: C
options.body: An orchestration layer automatically routes to the next tool based on the order's status field.
options.rationale: There is no implicit orchestration layer picking tools from a field. The model drives tool selection.

options.label: D
options.body: The agent executes a tool sequence planned in full at the start of the request.
options.rationale: There is no committed upfront plan — the agent chooses each next step from the latest context.

stem: Simple fact-checking queries traverse all four subagents sequentially (40+ seconds), while complex comparative research benefits from the full pipeline. The query distribution is diverse and evolving. What is the most effective way to optimize for varying query complexity?

options.label: A
options.body: Have the coordinator analyze each query and dynamically decide which subagents to invoke based on its assessment of requirements.
options.rationale: Correct. Letting the coordinator LLM reason per-query and invoke only the needed subagents adapts naturally to an evolving, diverse distribution — the strength of the orchestrator pattern.

options.label: B
options.body: Implement pattern-based routing mapping query structure categories to predefined subagent combinations.
options.rationale: Pattern routing calcifies as the distribution evolves — new intents break the patterns and land on the wrong pipeline.

options.label: C
options.body: Create a fast-path for factual questions that bypasses subagents, routing everything else through the full pipeline.
options.rationale: A binary fast-path wastes the full pipeline on every moderately complex query that could have used a subset.

options.label: D
options.body: Train a query-complexity classifier on labeled history and retrain periodically.
options.rationale: A trained classifier needs labels, retraining, and drift monitoring — over-engineered when the coordinator can decide at runtime.

stem: The web search agent has gathered sources; the document analysis agent must now examine them. In the Claude subagent model, how does information typically flow between these two specialized subagents?

options.label: A
options.body: The coordinator receives the web search agent's output and includes the relevant findings in the prompt when invoking the document analysis agent.
options.rationale: Correct. In an orchestrator-worker pattern the coordinator is the hub — it collects each subagent's output and forwards the relevant parts into the next subagent's prompt.

options.label: B
options.body: The web search agent directly invokes the document analysis agent, passing sources as parameters.
options.rationale: Subagents are isolated and can't directly call siblings — that would tightly couple them and defeat the orchestrator pattern.

options.label: C
options.body: The agents communicate through an event-driven message queue with completion events.
options.rationale: Event buses aren't part of the Claude subagent model; subagents don't publish/subscribe to each other.

options.label: D
options.body: Both agents share a memory store the first writes and the second reads.
options.rationale: A shared store can be an optimization but isn't how subagents typically communicate, and it introduces stale-read problems.

stem: A developer asks the agent to investigate why an API endpoint intermittently returns 500 errors across a 200+ file codebase, tracing through routing, middleware, business logic, and database layers. What task decomposition approach is most effective?

options.label: A
options.body: Dynamically generate investigation subtasks based on what is discovered at each step, adapting the plan as the error path emerges.
options.rationale: Correct. Debugging is adaptive — each file read changes the most useful next step. Let the agent follow the evidence.

options.label: B
options.body: First build a comprehensive plan mapping all code paths before any exploration.
options.rationale: You can't plan a correct path for an unknown error without exploration; planning blind wastes time and misses the real failure path.

options.label: C
options.body: Define a fixed sequence of steps upfront and execute each regardless of intermediate findings.
options.rationale: A fixed pipeline wastes work on uninvolved layers and can lock the agent out of the real root-cause path.

options.label: D
options.body: Run parallel workers across all four layers simultaneously, then synthesize.
options.rationale: Fan-out helps once subtasks are well-scoped. Here they aren't — you'd pay 4× to look in three layers that aren't the problem.

stem: An engineer used Claude Code yesterday for a 2-hour investigation she named "auth-deep-dive". She's worked on three other codebases since. How should she resume that specific session today?

options.label: A
options.body: Use `--resume auth-deep-dive` to load that specific session by name.
options.rationale: Correct. `--resume` with the session name is designed for picking a specific prior session out of many by the name you gave it.

options.label: B
options.body: Use `--continue` to pick up where the most recent conversation left off.
options.rationale: `--continue` resumes the most recent session in the repo — but she's worked on three other codebases since, so the most recent isn't auth-deep-dive.

options.label: C
options.body: Use `--session-id` with the UUID from yesterday's transcript file.
options.rationale: Possible but cumbersome — hunting for the UUID when she already has the session name.

options.label: D
options.body: Start fresh and re-read the same files.
options.rationale: Wastes the two hours of accumulated context from yesterday.

stem: Logs show the agent handles `lookup_order` failures inconsistently — sometimes retrying 5+ times, sometimes escalating immediately, sometimes asking the user for clarification. The tool returns a uniform `{"isError": true, "content": [{"type":"text","text":"Operation failed"}]}`. What is the most effective improvement?

options.label: A
options.body: Enhance error responses with structured metadata: `errorCategory` (transient/validation/permission), an `isRetryable` boolean, and a description of the cause.
options.rationale: Correct. Give the agent category, retryability, and a human-readable cause — that replaces guessing with deterministic policy.

options.label: B
options.body: Add an `analyze_error` tool the agent calls after any failure to determine the category.
options.rationale: Adds a round-trip for something the original tool already knows. Put the metadata in the original response.

options.label: C
options.body: Implement exponential-backoff retries in the MCP server for all errors before returning.
options.rationale: Blanket retries hurt on permanent errors (order not found) and hide useful distinctions from the agent.

options.label: D
options.body: Add few-shot examples showing how to interpret error-message patterns.
options.rationale: If the tool returns 'Operation failed' for every failure, no amount of few-shots can extract category info that isn't there.

stem: Your `process_refund` tool returns transient technical errors (5%) and permanent business errors (12%, e.g. "exceeds 30-day window"). The agent wastes 3–4 turns retrying business errors that can never succeed. Both types currently return only a plain text message. What most reduces wasted retries while improving the customer-facing reply?

options.label: A
options.body: Return structured error responses with `retryable: false` for business errors plus a customer-friendly explanation for Claude to use.
options.rationale: Correct. A retryable flag tells Claude deterministically not to retry, and a ready-made message improves the outgoing reply — both problems fixed at once.

options.label: B
options.body: Add few-shot examples showing how to distinguish retryable errors by parsing message text.
options.rationale: Relying on the model to text-parse error strings is fragile — exactly the instability seen today.

options.label: C
options.body: Add a `check_refund_eligibility` tool that must run before every `process_refund`.
options.rationale: Adds a round-trip to every refund to guard 12% of cases, and doesn't help when refund fails for other business reasons.

options.label: D
options.body: Retry technical errors automatically at the tool level; pass business errors to Claude unchanged.
options.rationale: Hiding retries masks latency and takes the model out of recovery decisions; business errors still arrive as plain strings, so the customer reply doesn't improve.

stem: The agent must insert a helper function into the middle of a 150-line module. The Edit tool fails because `old_string` can't find unique text — the file has repetitive docstrings and structural patterns. What is the most reliable way to complete the insertion?

options.label: A
options.body: Use Read to load the file, add the function at the right location in memory, then Write the full file back.
options.rationale: Correct. When Edit's unique-match contract can't be satisfied in a repetitive file, fall back to Read → modify → Write.

options.label: B
options.body: Use Edit with a 30+ line `old_string` to guarantee uniqueness.
options.rationale: Long, brittle match strings frequently miss on whitespace or minor edits and fail confusingly.

options.label: C
options.body: Use Edit's `replace_all` on a common pattern, embedding the new function in the replacement.
options.rationale: `replace_all` mutates every occurrence — corrupting the whole file.

options.label: D
options.body: Use Bash to append the function to the end of the file with a heredoc.
options.rationale: Appending puts it at the wrong location; the requirement is to insert between two existing functions.

stem: An engineer asks the agent to find all callers of a function before removing it. It's defined in a core library but also exposed through wrapper modules that rename it (e.g. `calculateTax` becomes `computeOrderTax`). Which exploration strategy most reliably identifies all callers?

options.label: A
options.body: Read the library and wrapper modules to enumerate every exposed name, then Grep for each name across the codebase.
options.rationale: Correct. You must enumerate every alias the function is exposed under — otherwise renamed wrappers hide callers. Gather aliases, then grep each.

options.label: B
options.body: Grep for files importing from the library or wrappers, then read each to check usage.
options.rationale: Misses dynamic imports, re-exports, and indirect call chains, and scales poorly.

options.label: C
options.body: Grep for the function's original name across the codebase.
options.rationale: The original name won't appear where a wrapper renamed it — you'd miss a whole class of callers.

options.label: D
options.body: Search project documentation to find documented integration points.
options.rationale: Docs are incomplete and stale; you can't safely remove a function on documentation-level evidence.

stem: A team wants a personal convention in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, a project convention in the repo's `CLAUDE.md`, and a stricter rule that applies only inside `packages/api/`. How does Claude Code combine these?

options.label: A
options.body: All three load hierarchically — user, then project root, then the directory-level `CLAUDE.md` — with more specific scopes layering on top.
options.rationale: Correct. CLAUDE.md is hierarchical: user (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`), project (root `CLAUDE.md`), and directory-level files in subdirectories, each adding scope.

options.label: B
options.body: Only the project root `CLAUDE.md` is read; the others are ignored.
options.rationale: User and directory-level CLAUDE.md files are both honored — the hierarchy is the whole point.

options.label: C
options.body: The directory-level file replaces the project and user files entirely within that path.
options.rationale: Scopes layer, they don't wholesale-replace — the more specific file adds to (and can override) the broader ones.

options.label: D
options.body: You must use `@import` to combine them; otherwise only the last-modified file wins.
options.rationale: `@import` is for modular composition, not a requirement for the hierarchy to work, and there's no last-modified-wins rule.

stem: You're authoring a skill that should run with its own isolated context and only be allowed to use Read and Grep. Which SKILL.md frontmatter expresses this?

options.label: A
options.body: `context: fork` together with `allowed-tools: Read, Grep`.
options.rationale: Correct. `context: fork` gives the skill isolated context, and `allowed-tools` (hyphenated) restricts it to the named tools.

options.label: B
options.body: `context: shared` with `allowed_tools: [Read, Grep]`.
options.rationale: The guide's field is hyphenated `allowed-tools`, not `allowed_tools`, and `shared` context doesn't isolate.

options.label: C
options.body: `isolate: true` with `tools: Read, Grep`.
options.rationale: Those aren't the frontmatter field names; the fields are `context` and `allowed-tools`.

options.label: D
options.body: `fork: yes` with `argument-hint: Read, Grep`.
options.rationale: `argument-hint` documents expected arguments, not tool permissions; forking is set via `context: fork`.

stem: You're wiring Claude Code into CI to review PRs and need machine-readable output conforming to a fixed shape, with each run isolated from others. Which invocation fits?

options.label: A
options.body: Run headless with `-p`/`--print`, `--output-format json`, and a `--json-schema`, with session isolation per run.
options.rationale: Correct. `-p`/`--print` runs non-interactively, `--output-format json` + `--json-schema` give machine-readable conforming output, and isolated sessions keep CI runs independent.

options.label: B
options.body: Run interactively and scrape the terminal output with a regex.
options.rationale: Scraping interactive output is brittle; the CLI provides structured JSON output for exactly this.

options.label: C
options.body: Use `--continue` so each PR builds on the previous run's context.
options.rationale: CI runs should be isolated — sharing context across PRs leaks state and causes nondeterministic reviews.

options.label: D
options.body: Set `--output-format json` but omit `-p`, keeping the interactive REPL open.
options.rationale: Without `-p`/`--print` it won't run headless to completion in CI.

stem: Your extraction schema defines `property_type` as an enum ['house','apartment','condo','townhouse']. 8% of extractions fail because listings mention new types ("studio", "loft", "duplex", "tiny house") that keep appearing. What is the best long-term solution?

options.label: A
options.body: Add an "other" value to the enum plus a separate `property_type_detail` string field for specifics when "other" is selected.
options.rationale: Correct. Keeps the strong enum for common cases (clean downstream joins) while giving a well-typed escape hatch that preserves detail. Stable long-term.

options.label: B
options.body: Continuously expand the enum as new types appear and monitor for more.
options.rationale: Whack-a-mole enum maintenance — every new listing style risks another validation failure.

options.label: C
options.body: Change `property_type` to a free-form string and normalize in post-processing.
options.rationale: Loses the validation guarantee entirely and pushes normalization downstream with no canonical vocabulary.

options.label: D
options.body: Add few-shot examples mapping unexpected types to the closest existing enum value.
options.rationale: Forcing 'tiny house' into 'house' drops real distinctions downstream — silently lossy.

stem: With strict tool-use schemas, JSON syntax errors are gone, but 5% of extractions have valid JSON with empty required fields (citations, methodology). The info exists in the source but in varied formats — inline citations vs. bibliographies, methodology in dedicated sections vs. embedded in the intro. What's most effective?

options.label: A
options.body: Add few-shot examples demonstrating extractions from documents with varied structures — citations in different formats, methodology across section types.
options.rationale: Correct. The failure mode is the model not recognizing varied formats; concrete examples across the distribution directly raise recall on the 5%.

options.label: B
options.body: Retry the same request when validation detects empty required fields.
options.rationale: Retrying the same prompt won't teach the model to recognize methodology embedded in an intro — the capability is the gap.

options.label: C
options.body: Build a regex post-processor to scan for citation patterns and keywords.
options.rationale: Regex over prose is brittle, misses nuanced cases, and ships silently wrong data.

options.label: D
options.body: Make the fields optional and flag incomplete records for manual review.
options.rationale: Papers over the symptom — the fields really are required downstream; this just trades one problem for reviewer workload.

stem: You process two document types with the same schema: standard monthly reports (archived after processing) and urgent exception reports (must trigger alerts within 30 minutes). You want minimal API cost while meeting latency. How should you architect the pipeline?

options.label: A
options.body: Route standard reports to the Batch API for 50% savings, and urgent exception reports to the real-time Messages API.
options.rationale: Correct. Match latency profile to urgency: batch for the cheap bulk, real-time for the latency-sensitive exceptions. Minimizes cost while meeting SLA.

options.label: B
options.body: Submit everything to the real-time API for consistent latency.
options.rationale: Consistent but expensive — monthly reports don't need real-time and shouldn't pay for it.

options.label: C
options.body: Submit all documents to the Batch API and trigger delayed alerts for exceptions.
options.rationale: Batch has up to a 24-hour window; a 30-minute alert SLA can't be met through batch.

options.label: D
options.body: Queue everything and submit hourly batches, flagging urgent docs for expedited handling.
options.rationale: Hourly batches still ride the batch SLO and don't guarantee the 30-minute window.

stem: A customer raised three issues over one session (refund turns 1–15, subscription 16–30, payment update 31–45). At turn 48 they ask "What happened with my refund?" The conversation is near the context limit. What best maintains the agent's ability to address all issues?

options.label: A
options.body: Summarize earlier turns into a narrative description, keeping full message history only for the active issue.
options.rationale: Correct. Progressive summarization compresses stable resolved topics while keeping the active thread verbatim — the classic pattern near the context limit.

options.label: B
options.body: Rely on MCP tools to re-fetch relevant information on demand.
options.rationale: Re-fetching helps freshness but doesn't solve context length, and you lose what was actually said.

options.label: C
options.body: Extract structured issue data into a separate context layer.
options.rationale: A sidecar layer adds engineering and doesn't preserve the conversational narrative the customer expects.

options.label: D
options.body: Use a sliding window that retains the most recent 30 turns.
options.rationale: A pure sliding window silently drops the refund issue (turns 1–15) — exactly what the customer is asking about.

stem: In 30+ minute exploration sessions the agent starts giving inconsistent answers about code it discussed earlier, and engineers must re-explain modules. What is the most effective approach?

options.label: A
options.body: Have the agent maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings and re-read it for later questions.
options.rationale: Correct. A scratchpad offloads findings to durable storage the agent can re-read, giving a stable memory independent of how crowded the context window gets.

options.label: B
options.body: Switch to a higher-capacity model tier for a bigger context window.
options.rationale: A bigger window delays the problem but doesn't solve attention degradation over long, noisy contexts.

options.label: C
options.body: Automatically clear context every 15 minutes for a fresh start.
options.rationale: Wholesale clearing throws away valid findings — exactly the state engineers complain about re-establishing.

options.label: D
options.body: Pre-summarize all source files before exploration and load only summaries.
options.rationale: Pre-summaries lose the detail that makes exploration useful and often misrepresent the files that matter most.

stem: Final reports frequently contain claims without proper source attribution. The web search and document analysis agents attach citations correctly, but the synthesis agent loses track of which sources support which conclusions when combining findings. What's the most effective architectural change?

options.label: A
options.body: Require all subagents to output structured claim-source mappings that the synthesis agent must preserve and merge.
options.rationale: Correct. Explicit claim-source mappings are a first-class output the synthesis agent can merge deterministically — no attribution gets dropped during summarization.

options.label: B
options.body: Maintain full transcripts and add a citation-resolution agent to reconstruct attributions from logs.
options.rationale: Post-hoc log analysis is fragile and expensive, and still loses bindings when synthesis merges points from multiple sources.

options.label: C
options.body: Have the report generator use semantic similarity against original sources to reconstruct which claims came from where.
options.rationale: Similarity matching can attribute the wrong source when two sources say similar things — you want the model's original mapping.

options.label: D
options.body: Have the coordinator inject source-identifier prefixes into text before each handoff.
options.rationale: Prefix tokens inside prose get dropped, paraphrased, or hallucinated; structured mappings outside the prose are more robust.

stem: You're deciding when the agent should call `escalate_to_human`. Which approach most reliably identifies cases that genuinely require a human?

options.label: A
options.body: Instruct the agent to escalate when the customer requests a human, when the issue requires a policy exception, or when it cannot make meaningful progress.
options.rationale: Correct. Escalation is a judgment call about intent and progress — exactly what LLMs handle well. Clear natural-language criteria beat rigid rules on the long tail.

options.label: B
options.body: Escalate after three consecutive failed tool calls.
options.rationale: A hard retry count fires both too early (legitimate retries) and too late (obvious policy issues on the first call).

options.label: C
options.body: Use sentiment analysis and escalate when a frustration score exceeds a threshold.
options.rationale: Sentiment misses calm customers who need a human for a policy exception and over-escalates on stylistic language.

options.label: D
options.body: Build a rules engine mapping issue types, segments, and product categories to escalation decisions.
options.rationale: Rules engines break on the cases they weren't designed for — and support is full of those.
